questions.question: What does a Bernoulli distribution model?
options: The number of successes in many trials.
A single trial with two outcomes, success with probability p and failure with probability 1 minus p.
questions.explanation: A Bernoulli variable is one yes-or-no trial: 1 with probability p, 0 with probability 1 minus p. Counting the successes across n independent Bernoulli trials gives the binomial distribution, which builds directly on it.

questions.scenario: A model classifies 20 emails independently, each spam with probability 0.1, and you want the probability that exactly 3 are spam.
questions.question: Which distribution applies, and what must hold for it to be valid?
options: The uniform distribution, because each email is equally likely.
The binomial distribution, valid because there is a fixed number of independent trials, each with the same success probability and two outcomes.
The Pareto distribution, because spam is rare.
The normal distribution, because counts are always normal.
questions.explanation: Counting successes in a fixed number n of independent, identical two-outcome trials is exactly the binomial setting. Its criteria are: fixed n, independent trials, constant p, and binary outcomes. Here n is 20, p is 0.1, and you want the probability of 3 successes.
questions.misconception: A count of successes is binomial, not normal. The normal can approximate it only when n is large and p is not extreme.

questions.question: Why does the Bernoulli distribution matter in machine learning?
options: It models continuous target variables in regression.
It is used only in physics, not machine learning.
It underlies binary classification: a model outputs p, the probability of the positive class, and log loss comes from the Bernoulli likelihood.
It is the distribution of model weights.
questions.explanation: Binary classification treats each label as a Bernoulli outcome with success probability p predicted by the model. Maximizing the Bernoulli likelihood over the data is equivalent to minimizing log loss (binary cross-entropy), which is the standard objective for logistic regression and many classifiers.
